title: Romulus et Hersilia
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Amulius' soldiery rules, old Numitor recovers his kingdom through his grandson, and on the feast of the Palilia the walls of Rome go up; then Tatius and the Sabines make war, Tarpeia opens the citadel and dies under the arms heaped on her, and Juno unbars a gate for the attackers, while Venus, who alone notices, may not undo a god's act and instead has the Ausonian nymphs boil the spring of Janus across the road. The war ends not in a decision but in a treaty, with Tatius admitted to the kingship beside Romulus. When Tatius is dead and Romulus is giving one law to both peoples, Mars asks Jupiter to keep an old promise; Jupiter nods, Mars drives down to the Palatine and carries Romulus off, and the mortal part of him dissolves in the air like a sling-bullet. Juno then sends Iris to Hersilia, weeping for a husband she believes lost; a star falls, her hair takes fire from it, and Romulus catches her, changes her name along with her body, and calls her Hora.

sentences.t:
Proximus Ausonias iniusti miles Amuli
rexit opes, Numitorque senex amissa nepotis
munere regna capit,
sentences.l: Next, the soldiery of unjust Amulius ruled the Ausonian resources, and old Numitor takes, by his grandson's service, the kingdom he had lost,
sentences.i: Next the armed following of Amulius the unjust governed the wealth of Ausonia, and old Numitor recovers, by his grandson's doing, the kingship he had lost,
sentences.n: Proximus agrees with miles, not with any named king: the collective singular miles, “the soldiery”, is the subject, so what ruled next was the armed following of Amulius, and the usurpation is stated as a fact of grammar. Ausonias … opes is the accusative object of rexit, Ausonia being an old poetic name for Italy. amissa … regna is neuter plural, “the kingdom lost”, with nepotis munere standing between the adjective and its noun; munus is a duty performed as much as a present given. The tense turns from the perfect rexit to the present capit, and the presents run on through the next unit: Ovid compresses a whole succession into a bare list.

sentences.t:
festisque Palilibus urbis
moenia conduntur, Tatiusque patresque Sabini
bella gerunt, arcisque via Tarpeia reclusa
dignam animam poena congestis exuit armis.
sentences.l: and on the festal Palilia the walls of the city are founded, and Tatius and the Sabine fathers wage wars, and Tarpeia, the way of the citadel having been unbarred, puts off beneath heaped-up arms a life deserving of punishment.
sentences.i: and on the feast of the Palilia the city's walls are founded; and Tatius and the Sabine elders make war; and Tarpeia, once the road into the citadel had been unbarred, puts off under a heap of arms a life that had earned its punishment.
sentences.n: festis Palilibus is an ablative of time: the Palilia, the shepherds' feast of Pales on the twenty-first of April, kept as the birthday of Rome. patres is the word for senators, the “fathers”, here of the Sabines. arcis via … reclusa is an ablative absolute — a self-contained “with X done” phrase where English wants a clause — and you will meet it constantly in this poem. Tarpeia is the nominative subject standing outside that phrase: she is the Roman girl who opened the citadel to the Sabines and died under the arms they heaped on her. exuo is the verb for stripping off clothing, so exuit animam is “she put off her life”; the form is spelled alike in the present and the perfect, and the presents that run before it in this unit, conduntur and gerunt, make the present the natural reading. dignam … poena, “deserving of punishment”, is the poem's verdict on her, given in two words and not argued.

sentences.t:
Inde sati Curibus tacitorum more luporum
ore premunt voces et corpora victa sopore
invadunt portasque petunt,
sentences.l: Thereupon those sown at Cures, after the manner of silent wolves, press their voices down with the mouth and fall upon bodies conquered by sleep and make for the gates,
sentences.i: Then the men bred at Cures, in the way of silent wolves, hold their voices down in their mouths, fall on bodies that sleep has conquered, and make for the gates,
sentences.n: sati Curibus, “sown at Cures”, is the participle of sero used as a noun for the men of the Sabine town of Cures; Curibus is the place-form of the name, and the plural is only the shape the town's name takes, not a plurality of towns. tacitorum more luporum is an ablative of manner with its genitive wrapped round it — “in the way of silent wolves” — and the simile does the work of an adjective: they come in without a sound. ore premunt voces is literally “with the mouth they press their voices down”, that is, they keep quiet. corpora victa sopore gives the sleeping Romans a passive participle instead of a verb of sleeping, and the military word invadunt then treats them as ground to be assaulted.

sentences.t:
quas obice firmo
clauserat Iliades:
sentences.l: which the son of Ilia had closed with a strong bar:
sentences.i: which Ilia's son had barred fast:
sentences.n: quas is the relative picking up portas two words earlier in the same line, feminine accusative plural. Iliades is a patronymic — “son of Ilia” — and it is Ovid's name for Romulus here instead of the name itself; Ilia is his mother. He is called Iliaden again at 824, at the moment he is carried off. obice firmo is an ablative of means, obex being the bar that holds a gate shut, and the pluperfect clauserat sets the barring before the night attack.

sentences.t:
unam tamen ipsa reclusit
nec strepitum verso Saturnia cardine fecit.
sentences.l: one, however, she herself unbarred, and Saturnia made no noise with the hinge turned.
sentences.i: one of them, though, she unbarred with her own hand, and Saturnia made no sound as the hinge went round.
sentences.n: Saturnia, “the daughter of Saturn”, is Juno, and she is named only in the second clause — after the first verb, reclusit, and before the second, fecit — so the gate is open before the reader is told who opened it. unam is feminine accusative, “one [gate]”, answering portas above. ipsa marks that a goddess did it herself; the Latin Library prints the masculine ipse, which would need a male subject the sentence never supplies. verso cardine is another ablative absolute, and the point of nec strepitum … fecit is that the hinge did not give her away.

sentences.t:
Sola Venus portae cecidisse repagula sensit
et clausura fuit, nisi quod rescindere numquam
dis licet acta deum.
sentences.l: Venus alone perceived that the bars of the gate had fallen, and was going to close it, except that it is never permitted to gods to undo the deeds of gods.
sentences.i: Venus alone perceived that the gate's bars had fallen, and she would have shut it again — except that gods are never allowed to undo what gods have done.
sentences.n: cecidisse repagula is an accusative and infinitive after sensit: “that the bars had fallen”. clausura fuit is the future participle with fuit, a periphrastic that states what was about to happen and did not; the literal keeps the Latin's “was going to close”, where English would say “would have closed”. nisi quod is “except for the fact that”. deum is the shortened genitive plural for deorum, so acta deum are “the deeds of gods”, set against the dative dis, “to gods” — the same word twice in two cases, which is the whole point of the rule.

sentences.t:
Iano loca iuncta tenebant
naides Ausoniae gelido rorantia fonte:
sentences.l: Places joined to Janus, dripping with a cold spring, the Ausonian naiads held:
sentences.i: The naiads of Ausonia held a place adjoining Janus, wet with the dew of a cold spring:
sentences.n: Iano is a dative with iuncta, “joined to Janus”, that is, next to his shrine, whose double gates stood open while Rome was at war. loca … rorantia is neuter plural and is the object of tenebant, with five words between the noun and its participle, the verb and the subject among them. gelido … fonte is an ablative of means with roro, “to be wet with dew”. tenebant is imperfect: the nymphs were already there, the standing background against which the next sentence acts. naides keeps its Greek plural.

sentences.l: these she asks for help, nor did the nymphs hold out against the goddess asking just things, and they drew forth the veins and streams of their own spring;
sentences.i: these she asks for aid, and the nymphs did not hold out against a goddess whose request was just: they drew out the veins and streams of their own spring;
sentences.n: rogo takes two accusatives, has and auxilium — “she asks these for help” — and has looks back to the naiads named in the line before. sustinuere and elicuere are the poetic third-plural perfect, -ere for -erunt; you will meet this ending constantly in verse, and it is never an infinitive. sustineo here is “to withstand, hold out against”, so the negative means they gave way at once. iusta petentem is a participle agreeing with deam, with the neuter plural iusta, “just things”, as its object. In fontis … sui the possessive is pushed past the verb to the far side of it.

sentences.t:
nondum tamen invia Iani
ora patentis erant, neque iter praecluserat unda:
sentences.l: not yet, however, were the mouths of Janus, standing open, impassable, nor had the water blocked the way:
sentences.i: and yet the mouths of Janus, which stood open, were not yet impassable, nor had the water shut off the road:
sentences.n: ora is neuter plural, “mouths”, of the gateway of Janus, with invia, “not to be gone through”, as its predicate: the water is rising but has not yet made the passage impossible. Iani patentis is genitive, and patens is the standing description of the gates of Janus, kept open in time of war. praecluserat is pluperfect against the imperfect erant — the blocking has not happened yet, and the next unit is how it is made to happen.

sentences.t:
lurida supponunt fecundo sulphura fonti
incenduntque cavas fumante bitumine venas.
sentences.l: they place lurid sulphur under the fruitful spring and set the hollow veins alight with smoking bitumen.
sentences.i: they lay pale-yellow sulphur under the teeming spring and fire its hollow veins with smoking pitch.
sentences.n: suppono takes a dative of the thing put under, fecundo … fonti; the two adjective-noun pairs are woven through each other, lurida … sulphura threaded through fecundo … fonti with the verb inside them. luridus is the sickly yellow of sulphur, not a brightness. venas carries on the metaphor of 788: a spring has “veins”, and here they are the channels the fire is set in. fumante bitumine is an ablative of means, bitumen being natural pitch.

sentences.t:
Viribus his aliisque vapor penetravit ad ima
fontis,
sentences.l: By these forces and others the heat penetrated to the lowest parts of the spring,
sentences.i: By these means and others the heat worked its way down to the bottom of the spring,
sentences.n: viribus his aliisque is an ablative of means, and the vague “and others” lets Ovid stop cataloguing. vapor is heat or steam rather than smoke. ad ima fontis is “to the lowest parts of the spring”, ima being a neuter plural adjective used as a noun with a genitive hanging on it. The perfect penetravit closes the account of what was done; the next unit turns from narrative to address.

sentences.t:
et Alpino modo quae certare rigori
audebatis aquae, non ceditis ignibus ipsis!
sentences.l: and you waters, who just now were daring to contend with Alpine stiffness, you do not yield to the fires themselves!
sentences.i: and you waters, that a moment ago dared match yourselves against Alpine frost — now you do not yield even to fire itself!
sentences.n: Ovid turns aside from the story to address the waters themselves: aquae is a vocative and audebatis and ceditis are second person plural. This is apostrophe; he turns aside like this again at 805-806, to Romulus himself. modo here is “just now, a moment ago”, not “only”, and Alpino belongs across the intervening words to the dative rigori, not to modo. certare takes that dative of the thing contended with, “Alpine stiffness”, the cold of Alpine snow-water. ignibus ipsis is a dative with cedo: they yield nothing even to fire, the water being now as hot as what heated it. The relative quae is held back until two words of its own clause have gone by, and its antecedent aquae does not arrive until the second word of 795.

sentences.t: Flammifera gemini fumant adspergine postes,
sentences.l: The twin doorposts smoke with a flame-bearing spray,
sentences.i: The two doorposts smoke with a spray that carries flame,
sentences.n: gemini postes are the two jambs of the gate of Janus. flammifera … adspergine is an ablative of means split wide open, with gemini and the verb standing inside it: “with a flame-bearing sprinkling”, the spray of the now-boiling spring. flammifer is a compound of the kind Latin verse builds freely, flamma plus fero. The edition keeps its own spelling adspergine, where other texts print asp-.

sentences.l: and the gate, promised in vain to the unbending Sabines, was built up in front by the new spring, until the soldiery of Mars should put on its arms;
sentences.i: and the gate, promised to the hard Sabines for nothing, stood walled off by the new spring, until the soldiery of Mars could arm itself;
sentences.n: The passive promissa names no promiser; what it looks back to is the unbarring at 781-782, where Saturnia opened one of the gates Iliades had barred, so that the gate was as good as made over to the Sabines. nequiquam, “for nothing”, is the verdict on that: the way was opened and is shut again. rigidis is “stiff, unbending”, the Sabines' standing character. praestructa is “built in front of”, the spring itself doing the work of a barricade, with fonte … novo an ablative of means wrapped round the verb; fuit rather than est with the participle points at the state reached and not the act. dum with the subjunctive indueret is “until”, with the sense of waiting for something to happen, not the plain “while” that dum takes with the indicative. Martius … miles is the collective singular again, the soldiery of Mars, that is, the Romans — the same construction as miles in 772, and this time the god named inside it is Romulus' father.

sentences.t:
quae postquam Romulus ultro
obtulit, et strata est tellus Romana Sabinis
corporibus strata estque suis, generique cruorem
sanguine cum soceri permiscuit impius ensis,
sentences.l: and after Romulus of his own accord offered these, and the Roman land was strewn with Sabine bodies and was strewn with its own, and the impious sword mingled the son-in-law's gore with the father-in-law's blood,
sentences.i: and after Romulus offered battle unasked, and Roman ground was strewn with Sabine bodies and strewn with its own as well, and an impious sword mixed a son-in-law's gore with a father-in-law's blood,
sentences.n: quae is the connecting relative opening the sentence and picking up arma from the end of the line before — “and these [arms] …”; read a connecting relative as “and them”, never as a question. ultro is “unprompted, without being challenged”: Romulus does not wait to be attacked. strata est … strata estque is deliberate repetition with the enclitic hung on the auxiliary, and the two ablatives it governs, Sabinis corporibus and suis, stand one on each side of the repeated verb. generi and soceri are genitives singular of gener and socer, son-in-law and father-in-law: the Roman men had Sabine wives, taken in a seizure these lines never narrate, so the war is fought inside families, and that is what makes the sword impius — the word for a breach of the duty owed to kin, not for simple cruelty. cruorem is spilt gore and sanguine the blood in the body, one set in each half of the phrase, and cum stands after its noun, sanguine cum soceri for cum sanguine soceri, which is normal in verse.

sentences.t:
pace tamen sisti bellum nec in ultima tantum
decertare placet Tatiumque accedere regno.
sentences.l: yet it is agreed that the war be stopped by a peace, and not to fight it out only to the last extremities, and that Tatius come into the kingship.
sentences.i: still, they resolve that the war be halted by a treaty, that they will not simply fight on to the last, and that Tatius be taken into the kingship.
sentences.n: placet, “it is agreed”, governs three infinitive clauses: sisti (a passive infinitive, “that the war be stopped”), decertare, and accedere. pace is an ablative of means. in ultima is a neuter plural, “to the uttermost”, and decertare is to fight a thing right out to a decision; tantum, “only”, is what the negative bites on — not that they will not fight, but that they will not merely fight. The Latin Library reads ferro, “with the sword”, in place of tantum, which turns the clause into “not to fight it out to the end with the sword” and takes the “only” out of it altogether. accedere regno takes the dative, “to come to the kingship”: Tatius is joined to Romulus as co-ruler, which is why 805 can open with his death.

sentences.t:
Occiderat Tatius, populisque aequata duobus,
Romule, iura dabas,
sentences.l: Tatius had fallen, and you, Romulus, were giving laws made equal for the two peoples,
sentences.i: Tatius had fallen, and you, Romulus, were giving the two peoples one law between them,
sentences.n: The second apostrophe of this part: Romule is a vocative and dabas is second person — Ovid speaks to Romulus directly, as he spoke to the waters at 794-795. occido here is “to fall, to die”, and the pluperfect sets the death before the scene. aequata agrees with iura, “laws made equal”, and populis duobus is a dative of the persons they are made equal for: one law for Romans and Sabines together, which is the settlement arranged at 803-804.

sentences.t:
posita cum casside Mavors
talibus adfatur divumque hominumque parentem:
sentences.l: when Mavors, his helmet laid aside, addresses in such words the parent of gods and of men:
sentences.i: when Mars, his helmet set down, speaks in these words to the father of gods and men:
sentences.n: This is the inverted cum: the main event of the sentence arrives in the cum clause, so the shape is “you were doing X, when Y happened”. cum here is the conjunction and not the preposition: it stands displaced inside the phrase, so posita cum casside is cum posita casside and casside is governed by nothing. posita casside is an ablative absolute — Mars takes his helmet off to ask a favour. Mavors is the older, fuller form of the name Mars, and this part uses three names for him: Mavors here, Martius as an adjective at 798, and Gradivus at 820. adfatur is deponent, passive in form and active in sense, “he addresses”. divum is the shortened genitive plural of divi, and the correlative -que … -que means “both … and”, a mannerism of high verse.

sentences.t:
“Tempus adest, genitor, quoniam fundamine magno
res Romana valet et praeside pendet ab uno,
praemia (sunt promissa mihi dignoque nepoti!)
solvere et ablatum terris imponere caelo.
sentences.l: “The time is at hand, father, since the Roman state is strong upon a great foundation and hangs from one guardian, to pay the rewards (they have been promised to me and to a deserving grandson!) and to set him, taken from the earth, in heaven.
sentences.i: “The time has come, father — since the Roman state stands firm on a great foundation and hangs upon a single protector — to pay what was pledged (it was promised to me, and to a grandson who deserves it!) and to take him from the earth and set him in the sky.
sentences.n: The infinitives solvere and imponere depend on tempus adest, “it is time to …”, and they are held back until 811 by the causal quoniam clause and by the parenthesis; solvere is the first word of that line. fundamine is a rare noun for a foundation, in the ablative. The edition reads et praeside pendet ab uno, “and hangs from a single guardian”; the Latin Library reads nec, “and does not hang on a single guardian”, and the two pull the argument opposite ways — nec makes Rome's independence of Romulus the reason for taking him, et makes his singular support the reason for rewarding him. The parenthesis is Mars pressing his own claim, and dignoque nepoti is a dative: Romulus is Jupiter's grandson through Mars. ablatum, “taken away”, is a participle standing in for the object of imponere, with terris an ablative of separation and caelo a dative.

sentences.t:
Tu mihi concilio quondam praesente deorum
(nam memoro memorique animo pia verba notavi)
“unus erit, quem tu tolles in caerula caeli”
dixisti:
sentences.l: You once said to me, with the council of the gods present (for I remember, and with a remembering mind I marked down your dutiful words), “There will be one whom you shall lift into the blue of heaven”:
sentences.i: You said to me once, before the assembled council of the gods — for I remember it, and I set your faithful words down in a mind that keeps them — “There shall be one whom you will raise into the blue of heaven”:
sentences.n: The main verb dixisti waits until 815, three lines after the Tu that is its subject: the sentence holds the reader through an ablative absolute, a parenthesis and a quotation before it says what the act was. concilio … praesente is that ablative absolute, with quondam inside it and the genitive deorum left outside. memoro memorique is the same root twice over, Mars insisting he has not got the words wrong. pia verba are words that keep faith, pius being the word for a duty honoured. tolles is a future indicative inside Jupiter's own words, and in caerula caeli is a neuter plural adjective used as a noun, “the blue expanses”, with caeli hanging on it. Mars's speech, opened at 808, is still running here, and Magnus marks the words he quotes with the same signs as the speech itself, so 814 both opens and closes a quotation inside another one.

sentences.t: rata sit verborum summa tuorum!”
sentences.l: let the sum of your words be ratified!”
sentences.i: let the whole of what you said be made good!”
sentences.n: rata sit is a jussive subjunctive, “let it be ratified”, and ratus is the technical word for a thing confirmed and binding — which is why the same root returns at 818 as rata signa. summa verborum tuorum is “the total of your words”, the accountant's word for a sum: Mars asks that the promise be settled in full, as one settles a debt, and the metaphor is already there in praemia solvere at 810-811.

sentences.t:
Adnuit omnipotens et nubibus aera caecis
occuluit tonitruque et fulgure terruit orbem:
sentences.l: The all-powerful one nodded assent, and hid the air with blind clouds, and terrified the world with thunder and lightning:
sentences.i: The Almighty nodded his assent, hid the air behind blinding cloud, and struck the world with terror by thunder and lightning:
sentences.n: adnuo is to nod agreement, and the nod is the whole of Jupiter's answer: his only words in this part are the ones Mars has just quoted back at him. omnipotens stands alone as a noun, “the all-powerful one”. aera is the Greek accusative of aer, kept in its Greek shape. caecis carries both senses at once — clouds that cannot be seen through and clouds that leave the world unseeing — so “blind” is the word and “blinding” is what it does. tonitru is a fourth-declension ablative. Magnus's colon at the end of 817 points forward: the signs are given, and the next sentence is Mars reading them.

sentences.t:
quae sibi promissae sensit rata signa rapinae
innixusque hastae pressos temone cruento
impavidus conscendit equos Gradivus et ictu
verberis increpuit
sentences.l: and these things he perceived to be confirmed signs of the seizure promised to him, and, leaning on his spear, Gradivus undismayed mounted the horses pressed by the bloody pole and cracked with the stroke of the lash
sentences.i: and these he read as sure signs of the carrying-off promised him; then, leaning on his spear, Gradivus mounted without a tremor the horses the bloody pole bore down on, cracked the lash
sentences.n: quae is a connecting relative again, “and these things”, taking up the thunder and the lightning; it is the object of sensit, with rata signa as its predicate — “he perceived them as ratified signs”. The subject Gradivus is not named until the fourth word of 820, two lines after the verb sensit. rapinae is a hard word — the noun for a snatching away, a carrying off by force — and Ovid uses it of the abduction of Romulus into heaven that Mars has been promised. innixus takes the dative hastae. pressos temone cruento are the horses with the chariot pole bearing down on them, and the pole is bloody because this is the war god's team. impavidus is a predicate adjective doing the work of an adverb. ictu verberis increpuit is “he made a noise with the stroke of the lash”: increpo is intransitive here, the crack of the whip, not a blow landed on the horses.

sentences.t:
pronusque per aera lapsus
constitit in summo nemorosi colle Palati
reddentemque suo non regia iura Quiriti
abstulit Iliaden:
sentences.l: and, gliding forward through the air, he halted on the top of the hill of wooded Palatium and carried off the son of Ilia as he was rendering to his own Quiris laws that were not kingly:
sentences.i: and, sweeping headlong down through the air, he came to a stop on the crest of the wooded Palatine and carried off Ilia's son in the act of giving his own citizens laws that were nothing like a king's:
sentences.n: pronus is “leaning forward, headlong”, and describes the angle of the descent. lapsus is the participle of the deponent labor, active in sense, “having glided”; the verb and its compounds come again at 825 (dilapsum), 838 (delapsa) and 846 (lapsum). aera is the Greek accusative once more. in summo … colle is the idiom “on the top of the hill”, the adjective doing a noun's work, with nemorosi agreeing with the genitive Palati. reddere iura is the standing phrase for administering justice, and reddentem is an accusative participle agreeing with Iliaden at the end of the sentence: Romulus is taken in the middle of the act. suo … Quiriti is a collective singular dative, “to his own Quiris”, the Quirites being the body of Roman citizens. non regia iura says what the laws were not — not the arbitrary word of a king; the Latin Library reads iam regia, “laws now royal”, which reverses the point exactly. Iliaden is the Greek accusative of the patronymic used at 781.

sentences.t:
corpus mortale per auras
dilapsum tenues, ceu lata plumbea funda
missa solet medio glans intabescere caelo.
sentences.l: his mortal body dissolved away through the thin airs, as a leaden bullet, sent from a broad sling, is wont to melt away in mid-heaven.
sentences.i: his mortal body melted away as it went through the thin air, the way a lead sling-bullet, once loosed from the broad sling, will waste to nothing in mid-sky.
sentences.n: dilapsum is the participle of the deponent dilabor with est left out, which is normal: “fell apart, dissolved”. per auras … tenues is split around it. The simile is built of interlocked pairs: lata and funda stand on either side of plumbea, but plumbea belongs to glans, which does not arrive until the seventh word after ceu, and missa agrees with glans too. medio … caelo is “in mid-sky”. intabescere is to melt gradually away, and the belief the simile rests on is that a sling-bullet grew hot enough in flight to melt — which is what lets it stand for a body losing its mortal part on the way up.

sentences.t:
Pulchra subit facies et pulvinaribus altis
dignior, est qualis trabeati forma Quirini.
sentences.l: A beautiful form comes up in its place, and one worthier of the high couches; the form of Quirinus in his striped robe is such as this.
sentences.i: A beautiful shape takes its place, worthier of the high couches of the gods: the shape that Quirinus wears in his striped robe.
sentences.n: subit is “comes up from below, takes the place of”: what rises is not a changed body but another one put in its room. dignior takes its complement in the ablative, pulvinaribus altis — the pulvinar was the cushioned couch on which a god's image was laid at a feast given to the gods, so “worthier of the couch” means worthy to be worshipped. In est qualis … forma Quirini the subject of est is forma and qualis looks back to facies. trabeatus is “wearing the trabea”, the striped ceremonial robe; Quirinus is the name Romulus carries as a god, and nothing in these lines confers it on him — Ovid simply uses it, here and again at 834, 836 and 851.

sentences.t:
Flebat ut amissum coniunx, cum regia Iuno
Irin ad Hersiliam descendere limite curvo
imperat et vacuae sua sic mandata referre:
sentences.l: His wife was weeping for him as lost, when royal Juno orders Iris to come down to Hersilia by her curving path and thus to carry her commands to the empty woman:
sentences.i: His wife was weeping for him as one lost, when royal Juno orders Iris to come down her curving path to Hersilia and to carry her message, in these words, to the empty woman:
sentences.n: ut amissum is “as [one] lost”, an accusative participle with ut giving the light she weeps in: he is not dead, but she has no way of knowing it. The inverted cum again, as at 806. This is the same goddess who unbarred the gate for the Sabines at 781-782, there called Saturnia. Irin is the Greek accusative of Iris, and impero takes an accusative and infinitive here — Irin … descendere … et referre — which is poetic; prose would use ut with the subjunctive. limite curvo is the rainbow, named by its shape and not by its name. vacuae is a dative and a cold word: vacuus of a woman is “empty, unattached, without a husband”, and Juno applies it to Hersilia before telling her anything. Hersilia stands here in the Latin accusative Hersiliam; the Latin Library prints the Greek Hersilien, which is the form the edition itself uses at 839, as it uses the Greek nominative Hersilie at 848.

sentences.t:
“O et de Latio, o et de gente Sabina
praecipuum, matrona, decus, dignissima tanti
ante fuisse viri, coniunx nunc esse Quirini,
sentences.l: “O foremost glory both out of Latium and out of the Sabine race, matron, most worthy to have been formerly the wife of so great a man, now to be the consort of Quirinus,
sentences.i: “O chief ornament of Latium and of the Sabine people alike, lady, most worthy to have been the wife of so great a man before, and now to be the consort of Quirinus,
sentences.n: decus is neuter and praecipuum agrees with it, with the vocative matrona wedged between the adjective and its noun; matrona is the word for a married woman of standing, used here of a woman whose husband has just been taken from her. The doubled o et … o et is anaphora, and the two phrases claim her at once for both peoples the settlement of 803-804 joined. dignissima governs the infinitives fuisse and esse, a poetic construction where prose would write dignissima quae fuerit. coniunx is stated once, in the second limb, and has to be understood in the first as well — “worthy to have been [the wife] of so great a man” — with the genitive tanti … viri hanging on that understood word, tanti separated from viri by the line-end and by ante fuisse.

sentences.t:
siste tuos fletus et, si tibi cura videndi
coniugis est, duce me lucum pete, colle Quirini
qui viret et templum Romani regis obumbrat.”
sentences.l: stop your weepings and, if you have a care of seeing your husband, with me as guide seek the grove which grows green on the hill of Quirinus and overshadows the temple of the Roman king.”
sentences.i: stop your weeping, and if you long to see your husband, take me for guide and make for the grove that grows green on the hill of Quirinus and shades the temple of the Roman king.”
sentences.n: siste is the imperative of sisto, the same verb as the passive sisti at 803 — Juno stops the tears as the treaty stopped the war. cura videndi coniugis is the gerundive construction, not a gerund with an object: videndi agrees with the genitive coniugis, and English has to turn it round into “a care of seeing your husband”. si tibi … est is the dative of possession, “if you have”. duce me is an ablative absolute with no participle at all, a noun and a pronoun set side by side: “with me as guide”. The relative qui is held back to the start of 837, four words after its antecedent lucum. templum Romani regis is the temple of Quirinus, that is, of Romulus under his new name — the apotheosis Hersilia has not yet been told about.

sentences.t:
Paret et in terram pictos delapsa per arcus
Hersilien iussis compellat vocibus Iris.
sentences.l: She obeys, and, having glided down to earth through her painted arches, Iris addresses Hersilie with the words she was commanded to speak.
sentences.i: She obeys; and having slid down to earth along her painted arches, Iris speaks to Hersilie the words she was told to speak.
sentences.n: Paret has no expressed subject: Iris is not named until the last word of 839, so the Latin makes the reader wait out the whole sentence for her. delapsa is another deponent participle, active in sense. pictos … arcus is accusative plural, “the painted bows”, the rainbow described as more than one arch because it is banded. iussis vocibus is an ablative of means, “with commanded words” — the message is Juno's, and Iris adds nothing of her own. Hersilien keeps the Greek accusative ending here, where 830 had the Latin Hersiliam.

sentences.t:
Illa verecundo vix tollens lumina vultu
“o, dea, namque mihi nec, quae sis, dicere promptum est,
et liquet esse deam,
sentences.l: She, scarcely lifting her eyes, with a modest face: “O goddess — for it is not ready to my hand to say who you are, and it is plain that you are a goddess —
sentences.i: She, hardly raising her eyes, her look all modesty: “Goddess — for I cannot readily say who you are, and yet it is plain that you are a goddess —
sentences.n: There is no main verb until inquit in 842: the participle tollens hangs until then, and the reader is inside Hersilia's speech before being told that she is speaking. verecundo … vultu is an ablative of manner wrapped round lumina. quae sis is an indirect question and takes the subjunctive. promptum est is “it is ready to hand, it is easy”, and the nec that negates it stands immediately before the indirect question rather than beside the phrase it belongs to. liquet is impersonal, “it is clear”, with the accusative and infinitive esse deam and te, “you”, left to be understood — she cannot name the goddess but has no doubt that she is one. This is her only speech in the part.

sentences.t:
duc, o duc” inquit “et offer
coniugis ora mihi, quem si modo posse videre
fata semel dederint, caelum accepisse fatebor.”
sentences.l: lead, o lead,” she says, “and set my husband's face before me; and if only the fates shall have granted that I can see him once, I shall confess that I have received heaven.”
sentences.i: lead me, oh lead me,” she says, “and set my husband's face before me; if the fates once grant me only this, that I may see him, I shall own that I have received heaven.”
sentences.n: duc, o duc is the imperative doubled, and offer is the imperative of offero, which drops its ending as fer does from fero. inquit is placed inside the speech, which is why Magnus's marks close and open again around it. ora is a plural for a single face, normal in verse. quem reaches back to coniugis three words earlier and is the object of videre inside the si clause; the Latin Library prints quae. dederint is a future perfect in the protasis against the future fatebor in the apodosis — Latin is exact about which of two future events comes first, where English is content with a present. posse videre is what the fates would grant: not the sight, but the power to have it. caelum accepisse is an accusative and infinitive after fatebor, and caelum is the whole sky, not a place in it: she asks for one sight of her husband and calls it the gift of heaven.

sentences.t:
Nec mora, Romuleos cum virgine Thaumantea
ingreditur colles:
sentences.l: No delay: with the Thaumantian maiden she enters the hills of Romulus:
sentences.i: No waiting: in the company of the maiden daughter of Thaumas she sets foot on the hills of Romulus:
sentences.n: Nec mora is an idiom standing on its own without a verb, “and there was no delay”. virgine Thaumantea names Iris by her father Thaumas, and this part has now called her three ways: Irin at 830, Iris at 839, and the daughter of Thaumas here. ingreditur is deponent, active in sense, and its subject is Hersilia, not the goddess who leads her. Romuleos … colles is an adjective built from the name, “the Romulean hills”, meaning Rome, and the phrase is split around the whole ablative phrase and the line-end.

sentences.t:
ibi sidus ab aethere lapsum
decidit in terras, a cuius lumine flagrans
Hersilie crines cum sidere cessit in auras.
sentences.l: there a star, slipped down from the upper air, fell to the earth, and Hersilie, blazing as to her hair from its light, withdrew into the breezes together with the star.
sentences.i: there a star, sliding down out of the upper air, fell to earth, and Hersilie, her hair set alight by its glow, went with the star into the air.
sentences.n: crines is a Greek accusative of respect after flagrans: flagro is intransitive and flagrans is a present active participle, so crines cannot be its object — it names the part of her that burns, “blazing as to her hair”. You will meet this accusative constantly in this poem, hung on participles and adjectives of either voice wherever the Latin wants to say in what respect a thing is so. lapsum is the deponent participle again, active in sense. a cuius lumine hangs on sidus, “from whose light”. decidit is spelled alike in the present and the perfect; cessit beside it is unambiguously perfect, so both are taken as past here. cedo in auras is the mildest verb available for a woman carried up to heaven — “she withdrew into the air” — and the Latin never says who took her. Hersilie is the Greek nominative form of the name.

sentences.t:
Hanc manibus notis Romanae conditor urbis
excipit et priscum pariter cum corpore nomen
mutat Horamque vocat, quae nunc dea iuncta Quirino est.
sentences.l: Her the founder of the Roman city catches with hands she knows, and changes her ancient name along with her body, and calls her Hora — who is now a goddess joined to Quirinus.
sentences.i: The founder of the city of Rome catches her in hands she knows, and changes her old name along with her body, and calls her Hora: she is a goddess now, joined to Quirinus.
sentences.n: Hanc, “her”, is set first to hand the sentence on from the last. manibus notis is an ablative of means, and notis is “known” — known to her, which is the one warm word in the transaction. conditor Romanae urbis names Romulus by his office; this part has already called him son of Ilia (Iliades 781, Iliaden 824), Romulus (799, and the vocative Romule 806), the Roman king (837) and Quirinus (828, 834, 836). mutat governs nomen, with priscum … nomen split around pariter cum corpore: the body is changed and the name with it. Both verbs have him as their subject, but only vocat takes her as its object, with Horam as the name given: what mutat governs is nomen. Horam is the accusative of Hora, the goddess Hersilia becomes. The closing relative clause quae nunc … est is the aetiological sign-off, stepping out of the story to the cult as it stood in Ovid's own day, and iuncta Quirino, “joined to Quirinus”, gives the new goddess her place by naming her husband.
